opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think the value of the robotics work was a little different from what we thought it was at the time. When we started, the goal was very ambitious: build a general-purpose robot hand that could learn to manipulate objects the way humans do. And we did get some remarkable results, like the hand solving a Rubik's cube, trained entirely in simulation and transferred to the real world.

But the deeper lesson was about what actually drives progress. We learned how powerful it is to take a general learning algorithm and just scale it up: more compute, more varied environments, things like domain randomization so the model couldn't overfit to the quirks of the simulator. That idea, that you get robustness and generalization by throwing a huge diversity of experience at a big model, turned out to be the same lesson that was playing out in language models.

The hard part about robotics was data. In simulation you can generate a lot of it, but the gap to the real world is always there, and collecting real-world robot data is slow and expensive. Meanwhile, with language, the internet had already done the data collection for us. So at some point it became clear that the fastest way to make progress on general intelligence wasn't through robotics, at least not then.

So I see the robotics work as a really important training ground, both for the ideas and for the people. A lot of the engineering muscle we built there, running large-scale training and caring about infrastructure and reliability, carried directly into the work on GPT models. It wasn't a detour so much as the place where we learned how to do this kind of research at scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robotics being difficult and slow, but does not say the work was far from commercialization.

r002.rationale: It describes learning and scaling as a lesson from the work, but identifies the project’s goal as building a general-purpose robot hand, not demonstrating machine learning’s power.

r003.rationale: It says the lesson about scaling learning across diverse experience was also playing out in language models and that robotics engineering carried into GPT work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I came to OpenAI, one of the first things I worked on was the robotics team. And at the time, I think a lot of people, including me, honestly, thought about robotics as the end goal. Like, if you want to build AGI, you need something that can act in the physical world. That was the framing.

But what the robotics work actually taught us was something a little different. We had this project where we trained a robot hand to solve a Rubik's Cube, and the hard part was never really the manipulation itself. The hard part was the data. Simulation only gets you so far, and real-world data is incredibly slow and expensive to collect. You're running one physical robot, it breaks, you fix it, you get a few hours of experience. Meanwhile, over on the language side, you've got the entire internet sitting there.

So the real value of that work, looking back, was that it clarified where the leverage was. It showed us that the techniques, the scaling, the reinforcement learning, the sim-to-real stuff, all of that was sound. The ideas worked. But the bottleneck was data, and language had the data. That's a big part of why we made the decision to wind down robotics and put those people onto what became GPT-3 and the models after it.

And I'd say the other value was the people. That team was incredibly strong, and a lot of them went on to do foundational work on the language models. So even though the robots themselves didn't ship, the robotics work ended up being one of the most important things we did, just not in the way we expected.

r002.rationale: It says the robotics work tested techniques that proved sound, but does not identify demonstrating machine learning’s power as the work’s purpose.

r003.rationale: The response says robotics techniques and team members contributed to GPT-3 and later language models.

astra-6.text: For me, the value was in working on intelligence in a setting where you couldn’t avoid the real world. A robot has to perceive what’s around it, decide what to do, and then act—and if it gets something wrong, that becomes very clear. That made robotics a useful way to think about how the pieces of an intelligent system fit together. Even when the immediate application was limited, the underlying questions felt much broader.

sol-6.1.text: I saw robotics as a way to work on intelligence in a very concrete setting. You had to build something that could perceive the world, make decisions, and then deal with the consequences of those decisions. A lot of the value was in discovering how much we were still missing. You could get a robot to do something impressive in a carefully controlled environment, but getting it to generalize was a much harder problem. That helped shape how I thought about AI: the goal had to be systems that could learn and adapt, rather than systems where we engineered every behavior by hand.
